The experiment servers have a tool called beam installed.

This tool can be used to compress and upload a folder and later download and decompress it.

The advantage of beam is that it does not need to create a temporary file during upload or download (in contrast to manually creating a compressed archive with tar and then uploading that), allowing uploading even if the compressed archive would not fit on the disk at the same time as the uncompressed files.

To upload a folder use: 
 beam up <path to your folder>
This will create and upload a file with a name like folder-timestamp.tar.zstd.

To download a file use 
 beam down <filename>

To see available files use 
 beam list
This will download and extract the folder in the current working directory.

docker build \
 --build-arg endpoint="https://databus.dbpedia.org/repo/sparql" \
 --build-arg default_graph="http://sparql.uni-paderborn.de:8891/dbpedia" \
 --build-arg buffer_memory="16384" \
 -t databus-dbpedia-virtuoso .

Docker has two main concepts called image and container.

A image is a template, it should contain everything needed to run an application.

A container is a running instance of an image, it can contain working state and other runtime artifacts of an application.
Follow the official Docker install instructions here: https://docs.docker.com/install/

section: Docker > Creating a Docker image from your application / demo > Basics
text:
A Docker image is created by the Docker daemon following the steps in a Dockerfile.

The full documentation of a Dockerfiles syntax can be found here: https://docs.docker.com/engine/reference/builder/

section: Docker > Creating a Docker image from your application / demo > Choosing a base image
text:
First of all you have to choose a base image on which to build your own image.

For example, if you have a java application you should use the OpenJDK Docker image.

There are also images of various Linux Distributions such as Ubuntu or Debian.

Also choose the right tag for your base image. If your application runs on Java 8, use an image with Java 8 (for example openjdk:8)

In the following we will need two different base images: One for the build environment and one for the runtime environment.

section: Docker > Creating a Docker image from your application / demo > The build environment
text:
In the following we will use the example of a Java application using the Maven build system.

The base Image we will use for our build environment will be maven:3-jdk-8.

To start our Dockerfile we now write

FROM maven:3-jdk-8 AS builder.

FROM tells Docker which base image we want to use, the AS builder part assigns the name builder. This will become important later.

To build our application we first have to copy our source code into the running container.

We do this by writing ADD . /example.

This will copy the Docker build context into the folder /example inside the container.

Next we will need to change our working directory to the newly created directory containing our application code.

We do this by writing WORKDIR /example.

Now we need to build our application.

We do this by writing WORKDIR /example.

Now we need to build our application.

In this case, since we are building a maven application, we just need to write RUN mvn package into our Dockerfile.

RUN tells Docker to run the given command inside the container.

To make the next part easier we will now rename the resulting jar file, by writing RUN mv target/*.jar target/example.jar.

section: Docker > Creating a Docker image from your application / demo > The runtime environment
text:
To keep the final download size of our image small, we should only add anything needed to run our application.

For example, we don't need maven to run our application.

In this example we will use openjdk:8 as our base image, so we will write FROM openjdk:8 into our Dockerfile.

Next we need to copy the build application from the build environment into the runtime environment.

We do this by writing COPY --from=builder /example/target/example.jar /example.jar.

This will copy the file /example/target/example.jar from the build environment to the runtime environment at the path /example.

Now we just need to tell Docker how to start our application.

We do this by writing CMD java -jar /example.jar.

The CMD tells Docker to execute the given command to start our application.

section: Docker > Creating a Docker image from your application / demo > Building the image
text:
Now we have everything in our Dockerfile and are ready to build our image.

To do this execute the command sudo docker build . in a terminal.

This will tell Docker to build an image using the current directory as build context.

If everything went well you should see a message similar to Successfully built b0fe6648c8ff.

We can now run the image by running the sudo docker run b0fe6648c8ff command.

If your application listens to connections on some port(s) you need to add those to the command, like this sudo docker run -p 8080:8080 b0fe6648c8ff.

text: When does the sick note have to be submitted to the employer if you feel a bit unwell on Friday and stay at home, but are still ill on Monday? If the weekend is between two sick days, it counts towards the three-day period - because it's about calendar days, not working days. This means that if you stay home sick from Friday and are still unfit for work on Monday, the certificate must be submitted to your employer on Monday - even if Saturday and Sunday are days off for you. However, if your doctor's only sends the eAU to the health insurance fund in the afternoon or evening on Monday, your employer may not be able to retrieve it until Tuesday. If you have private health insurance, you are also still obliged to send the sick note to your employer yourself. This can quickly become stressful.

page_title: Leaving Germany to live in another EU country
text:
Most agencies require a three months -at least- written notice to terminate your contract.

Your preferable termination date must be at least 3 months from the day you send the letter.
For example, if you send your letter at 15th August 2019 to e.g. the electricity company, the first available date to ask for termination will be 16th November 2019. 
Additionally, you need to check your contract regarding the delay between the letter and the ending of the contract. There are cases that the termination can take place at the end of requested month e.g. November 2019, and not the 16th. In case you receive a termination date that violates your contract, send them a letter back mentioning the contract. Otherwise, you will have to comply. You can try to ask for an earlier than 3 months termination, but your chances of success a low to non-existent.

section: Letter of Intent (LOI) > What is a Letter of Intent?
text: For some projects, the project sponsor requires a declaration of intent from the consortium partners and participating companies in the form of a "Letter of Intent" (LOI). In this letter, the relevant party confirms that it will participate in the project and contribute to it if funding is granted.

section: Letter of Intent (LOI) > How is such a letter of intent structured?
text:
A letter of intent usually consists of three parts. 
 a brief description of the company and its expertise
 a substantive explanation of why the planned project suits the company in question, how the company can contribute to the planned project and how the company can also benefit from the project
 confirmation that the company will be involved if the project is funded.

The letter of intent should be inserted on the official letterhead and signed with the original signature.

Our Matrix server (chat.dice-research.org) is only available for the members of ZIM groups ag-ngonga and dice-chat-users.

However, people from other Matrix servers can be invited to any chat. UPB computer science department has their own server: https://element.cs.uni-paderborn.de/ - which is also integrated with IMT accounts and available for all CS students. Clients are listed at https://matrix.org/clients/
 The default client is Element (find it at https://element.io/).

Note: This assumes you are using the Riot.im client. If you are using a different client, it will look differently.

Once the client is opened, click on the “Sign in” button.

In the dialog there is the text “Sign in to your Matrix account on matrix.org”. Next to this text there is a “Change” Button.

Once you click this button there should be a text field labeled “Homeserver URL”. Enter the URL https://chat.dice-research.org in this field. This will use our own Matrix server instead of the default one.

After that, click on next, enter your IMT username and password and click on “Sign in”.
You are automatically added into the main and offtopic group chats.

section: Starting a Chat with a Person
text:
To start a chat with a person you will have to enter their Matrix id.
A Matrix id consists of the username and the homeserver URL.
In our case id will look like this:
@<username>:chat.dice-research.org
Matrix uses this id format to enable users on different servers to chat with each other.
To start a chat with a person on another Matrix server, enter their Matrix ID. You can find your own Matrix ID by clicking on your name in the top left corner.
You might also be able to add a user via their E-Mail address, if they have enabled discovery via their E-Mail address.
This can be done via the settings.
You are always able to find a user with their id.

section: Inviting a Person into an existing Room
text:
To invite a Person to a Room, click the "Invite Person" Button at the top of the member list on the right side of the Riot window.

A small window will open. You can search for a Person to invite here.

Again you can find a Person by their Matrix ID, E-Mail (if they set it) or via their Name (if you share a different Room with them).

To invite a Person from a different Homeserver, just enter their Matrix ID.

After you added the Person(s) you want to invite press the "Send invite" Button.

The Riot client will use Jitsi to start Group voice and video calls.

To start a Jitsi conference simply click the voice or video call button on the right of the message textbox.

It should add a Jitsi Widget to the room, which will open a conference on our own Jitsi server.

Do not use the Jitsi Widget found under "Manage Integrations", it will use the Jitsi server provided by Riot.im.

section: 5. Paper Presentation > Fix for laggy PDF produced by beamer
text:
When you use our official latex beamer template you are likely to come across laggy pdfs due to resolution of embedded bitmap images.

You can fix this by applying this command to your final pdf:

$ gs -sDEVICE=pdfwrite -dCompatibilityLevel=1.4 -dPDFSETTINGS=/printer -dNOPAUSE -dQUIET -dBATCH -sOutputFile=slides_reduced.pdf slides.pdf

You can also shrink your embedded images in the beginning.
See the image resolution:
$ identify DICE_White.png
DICE_White.png PNG 11790x5309 11790x5309+0+0 8-bit sRGB 378853B 0.000u 0:00.000

This image is way too big and needs to be resized:
$ mogrify -resize 10% DICE_White.png

You will not always see this with ls -h, since e.g. png compression largely reduces file sizes of monochromatic images as above but when it gets embedded in pdf this compression is sometimes lost.

Getting a PhD hat is a passiv process

Preliminary version from March 1, 2019

For receiving the PhD grade from the UPB, there are two major steps required.

The PhD board has to check whether the student fulfills the prerequisites for a PhD. The required documents can be found on the UPB web page(at the bottom of the page).

Based on the submitted documents, the PhD board will decide whether you are allowed to submit your thesis.

After a positive response from the PhD board, you can register yourself as student of the university. Note that this is not mandatory and you are free to decide whether you want to become a student or not.

Read here more about the supervision agreement between you and your supervisor.
After the PhD board admitted the student, the PhD thesis can be submitted. The required documents can be found on the UPB web page(at the bottom of the page).
See 'Promotion' at https://cs.uni-paderborn.de/en/studies/audit-matters

It became a tradition of the DICE group that a PhD student receives a special (funny) PhD hat after they successfully pass their defense. This PhD hat should be tinkered by members of the DICE group (ideally, without the PhD student noticing). The hat is given to the PhD student (the target) directly after the successful defense so that they can wear it when making photos. It typically comes with a card and a gift.

The group chooses a hat agent, i.e., a person responsible for creating the hat. This may be the PhD student that is most likely the next student to defend their thesis. However, the process is not well defined.

Creating the hat typically needs to be planned. The hat agent may organize meetings with group members that know the target well and create a list of possible topics that might be possible to be covered by the hat. Typical points that are covered by a hat are the following (this is a non-exhaustive list):
 Research topic of the target
 Figures or objects from the thesis (or related to it)
 Figures or objects from papers (or related to them)
 Objects / Logos related to tools that the target implemented or worked with
 Objects / Logos related to projects that the target worked on
 Countries that the target visited during their PhD
 Objects related to the personality of the target
 Hobbies
 Food
 Habits
 Events that happened during the PhD

The hat agent typically orders a hat that is used as "basement". Especially the top but also the sides of the hat may be decorated. A group of volunteers creates and adds the decorations based on the previous discussions. This is typically done together in one or several sessions.

It might be a good idea to create an own private chat room for the hat creation process and invite everybody, except the target.
 The hat agent should organize the card that can be signed by group members. Note that not all group members are always available. Hence, a period of 2 weeks is a good way to ensure that a lot of people can sign the card.
 Over the whole creation process, the hat agent should keep track of costs that they had to cover.
 The hat agent should also start to collect money from group members as soon as the card can be signed. The money has two purposes: 1) it should cover the costs of the hat and 2) it should be used for a gift (typically, a voucher) that is given to the target together with the hat and the card.

Getting Started:

Find a suitable call that matches the scientific ambition and strategic goals of your idea. A list of platforms with national and EU funding opportunities is available here. 
 Reach out to colleagues who could contribute scientifically, technically or through use cases.
 Analyse the call in depth and map your concrete ideas, methods and expected results to the expected outcomes, the scope, and the impact requirements of the call.
 Seek support from DICE Research Management (for instance, w.r.t. funding rules, call requirements, forms and budgets, consortium data, ethics and data management, timelines and submission logistics).
 Streamline your proposal writing workflow (see image for the time frame and steps recommended for an EU grant application).

Further tips on the individual steps and sections of an EU grant application can be found below.

Horizon Europe is structured in three program pillars (Pillar I: Execellent Science, Pillar II: Global Challenges and European Industrial Competitiveness, Pillar III: Innovative Europe). You can find more information here.

Before finalising your consortium, verify the eligibility status of all partner countries.
Consult the official list of EU Member States and Associated Countries in the Horizon Europe Programme Guide here. 
Associated Countries are generally fully eligible for EU funding. No national co-funding is required. They have the same rights and obligations as EU partners (e.g. funding rates, reporting requirements, contractual rules), as they contribute to the Horizon Europe budget. However, eligibility may vary depending on the specific call. Some calls include additional geographical requirements or restrictions. Always check the call text carefully.
 Note that some countries are associated only to specific programme parts (Pillars)

SSH

All IRB managed VMs and Servers as well as most other VMs and Servers can be reached via SSH (Secure SHell).

There are different methods that can be used to authenticate to an SSH server, the two most common being passwords and ssh keys.

While passwords are self-explanatory, ssh keys are not.

SSH keys work by using a public and private key scheme, where the server knows the public key(s) for a user and the client proves possession of the private key.

To generate a key pair use the ssh-keygen -t rsa -b 4096 command.

This generates an 4096 bit RSA key pair.

You can either do this by hand or use the ssh-copy-id <user>@<server> command.

To install the key by hand you have to copy the contents of the ~/.ssh/id_rsa.pub file into the ~/.ssh/authorized_keys file on the server(s) you want to login to.

The public key file will contain one line text that will look like this ssh-rsa AAAAB3Nz[...]SlNt0jtkEr1Q29SD/ <user>@<hostname>.

Append this line to the ~/.ssh/authorized_keys file on the target server(s).

You might have to create the file and folder.

Another authentication method is kerberos.

Kerberos works by authenticating to a central server (for example with a password) in exchange for a ticket.

This ticket can then be used to login to the target server (if it has been setup for kerberos auth).

All IRB managed VMs and Servers are setup for Kerberos auth.

To setup your local system for Kerberos refer to this page: https://hilfe.uni-paderborn.de/Single-Sign-On_einrichten_unter_Linux

It boils down to executing
sudo apt install krb5-user; sudo wget -4 https://download.uni-paderborn.de/pc/configs/kerberos/krb5.conf -O /etc/krb5.conf
once and then using kinit <imt login> to login.

To use Kerberos with ssh, add the -K flag to your command.

Example: ssh -K raki.cs.upb.de

section: Important Information for IRB managed VMs and Servers
text:
By default IRB managed VMs and Servers do not allow password auth.

Instead SSH keys or Kerberos should be used.

To setup your SSH key(s) you can connect via the IRB sshgate (ssh <imt user name>@sshgate.cs.upb.de), it will automatically authenticate you using Kerberos.

You can then connect to your desired target and insert your public key into the ~/.ssh/authorized_keys file.

section: Copying files from and to servers
text:
The usage of ftp to transfer files is discouraged, as the protocol does not support encryption of files or credentials.

Instead something like sftp should be used.

section: Copying files from and to servers > scp
text:
For simple file transfers, `scp` (Secure CoPy) can be used.

You can use it like this `scp <source> <target>`, where source and target are a local path and a remote path in the form of `<username>@<server>:<path>`.

For example, to copy a file named `example` in the current directory to your home directory on a server use `scp example user@server:~/`.

To copy the file back to your current directory you can use `scp user@server:~/example ./`

section: Copying files from and to servers > rsync
text:
A more advanced utility is `rsync`.

rsync uses the same path notation as `scp`, but has more features.

`rsync` compares source and destination files and only transfers the difference between the two.

This can be very useful if you are transferring very large files over a unstable connection, as `rsync` can resume the transfer.

For rsync to work, it has to be installed on both systems.

However all IRB managed servers, as well as most other servers have `rsync` installed.

By default `rsync` is silent.

To enable a progress report, call `rsync with the `-P` flag.

To copy a whole directory use the `-r` flag.

Important note: Unlike the GNU corutils `cp` command, `rsync` uses the BSD convention for paths.

A trailing slash on a path will copy the contents of that directory, instead of the directory itself.

For more information on `rsync` see `man rsync`

Dissemination is important to generate visibility. Sharing our research results, our papers and conference attendance publicly can have a number of benefits: more people become aware of us and our research group becomes better known; we have a larger pool of applicants for our job advertisements; your papers get more attention and thus perhaps more citations; especially in externally funded research projects, it is important to show research activity - just to name a few advantages.

section: Twitter > I have something that could be interesting for social media, what do I have to do?
text: If you want to share content, let us know in Matrix chatroom DICE Dissemination or send a message to Franzi. You don't have to have a finished tweet, it's enough if you want to share an idea. Franzi usually takes care of the wording of the tweet and a fitting graphic.

section: Twitter > What content is suitable for social media?
text:
Papers accepted at conferences
 Software releases with nice features
 Projects and interesting news
 Contents listed at the DICE website: new demos, paper awards, new job positions
 Ideally, one of your papers will generate several posts: 1. at the acceptance at the conference, 2. at the presentation at the conference, 3. at the publication after the conference. We are also happy to present your paper in more detail in a multi-part tweet, for which you must provide some information and a graphic.

section: Twitter > I don't have a Twitter account yet, how can I get started?

Don’t have a Twitter account you want to use for work? Create one and follow @DiceResearch.
 Good news: There is already a community, you can follow some of your colleagues.
 Good news again: As you are working on your tasks, you’ve probably already become an expert for others. Share your knowledge and connect with other researchers!
 Don’t have contents? Don’t worry.
 Start with checking tweets of @DiceResearch and like them if you like them.
 If you really like tweets, retweet them.
 If you really like tweets and have additional information, add a comment to the respective tweet or retweet as a quote and add contents.
 Don’t want to use Twitter? No problem. If you have contents to publish, just collect the required data (see below) and post it in Matrix chatroom SocialMedia. We will take care.

To further expand our Twitter account @DiceResearch and grow our network, we need your input! Therefore, we would be happy if each of you prepares content for at least 2 tweets, so that we can regularly provide the account with interesting insights from the DICE Group. The tweets don't have to be "Twitter ready" yet, I'll do the editing of the tweet. Here are 10 ideas for content:
1. Project Introduction – #DICEprojects
Briefly tell us about the research project you are working on. What are you researching? What are the goals? Are there any particularly interesting results? A logo or group photo for the tweet would also be great. 2. Papers – #DICEreadme

Working hours
 A student assistant can have up to 19 working hours per week. section: Why do timesheets have to be filled out?
text: In many research projects, the funding body requires timesheets to be kept on the work in the project. It is important that these are filled out and archived carefully, as the documents can be checked in the event of an audit and, in the worst case, funding may have to be returned if it is not clear what work was carried out for the project in question.

section: Where can I find the timesheet template?
text: Paderborn University provides templates for the timesheets for the current year under this link (only available from the university network). If you are not sure which template is the right one, please ask your supervisor or the coordinator of the project you are funded by.

section: What is important when filling out the timesheet?
text: The maximum limits of the Working Hours Policy and the Working Hours Act must be observed. Accordingly, working hours of more than 10 hours per day are not permitted. Hours recorded on weekends and public holidays are not permitted. Tip: We recommend recording the average contractual working time per week. Overtime cannot be claimed with the Granting Authority. Absences (e. g. vacation, illness, parental leave, maternity leave) are to be indicated with the working time "0" and marked with the keyword "absent" / "abwesend". You do not have to give the exact reason, it is sufficient to describe the day as “absent”. Tip: Make sure that your absences in the timesheet are absolutely identical with the leaves and days off that you reported to the Human Resources Department. section: UPB Business Travel (Dienstreisen) > How to get your business trip financed
text: Agree with your project lead or supervisor about you travel plans. You get a empty VM and are responsible for installing an OS of your choice.

You will need to manage OS updates and upgrades by yourself. Otherwise, the VM will be shut down if the software would get outdated.

It's a good idea to include a reference to your project and/or purpose of the VM in the hostname.

Namespace is also shared with everyone else in the CS department, so it might be a good idea (but not mandatory) to start your name with dice-.

Automated reboots
IRB managed VMs automatically reboot for security updates and similar reasons.

The process as mentioned at 2023-06-02 is: "Whenever a server needs to reboot, the administrative and the technical contact will be reminded after 1 and 5 days. After a week, the server will be rebooted if no one is working on it."

It is suggested to use systemd-inhibit if you need to disable automatic reboot.
